We established a real-world, multicentre benchmark using 527 patients from three hospitals with fully paired PSMA PET, CT, T2-weighted MRI, and diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI), together with pathology-confirmed biopsy labels. Models were developed in one centre ( n = 363) and independently evaluated in two external centres ( n = 164). We compared frozen pretrained encoders, fine-tuned 2D and 3D CNN and Vision Transformer models, three fusion strategies, and an interpretable cross-modal Transformer. PSMA PET provided the greatest incremental value, with its removal producing the largest AUC reduction internally (−0.077) and externally (−0.055), supported by the highest attention attribution (αPET = 0.45). PSMA PET/CT also outperformed mpMRI externally (AUC 0.753 vs. 0.653). DWI was the principal source of domain shift, as its exclusion improved external AUC by 0.079 amid inter-centre b-value heterogeneity. Intermediate fusion performed most consistently internally, whereas late fusion and pretrained 2D models generalised better externally. This benchmark supports robust, non-invasive csPCa diagnosis by identifying modalities and fusion strategies that generalise reliably across institutions.

title: GliaDose: An alternative approach for clinical CAR-T dose prediction via PBPK–glioblastoma-on-a-chip integration
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) is a highly aggressive brain tumor with poor prognosis and limited treatment options. Chimeric antigen receptor T cell (CAR-T) therapy has emerged as a promising immunotherapy for GBM. However, unlike conventional drugs, CAR-T cells are living therapeutics that exhibit non-linear pharmacokinetics, expansion, and complex tissue trafficking, making conventional animal-to-human dose extrapolation unreliable. Furthermore, species-specific differences and the vasculature limit the translational relevance of preclinical models. To address these challenges, we developed GliaDose, a hybrid framework that integrates physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling with a vascularized glioblastoma-on-a-chip (GoC) platform to support quantitative first-in-human dose (FIHD) prediction for CAR-T therapy. The PBPK model was parameterized exclusively with human physiological data and incorporates a brain-tumor compartment to explicitly capture CAR-T transport across the vasculature. Complementarily, the GoC platform recapitulates key features of the GBM microenvironment, including three-dimensional tumor architecture, extracellular matrix, and perfusable human vascular networks, enabling assessment of CAR-T transmigration under flow conditions. Integration of GoC-derived efficacy data into the PBPK framework enabled quantitative dose–response predictions and identified vascular barriers as critical determinants of CAR-T tumor access. GliaDose provides a human-relevant, mechanistic alternative to animal-based dose selection and may improve FIHD prediction and personalized CAR-T therapy for GBM.

title: Radiographer fracture detection with and without AI assistance in prospective emergency department use
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems for fracture detection perform strongly in controlled settings, but prospective real-world evidence is limited. In a three-month deployment in one emergency department, thirteen radiographers in a radiographer-led screening programme independently interpreted 2496 consecutive musculoskeletal examinations (one radiographer per examination), reviewed output from a commercial deep-learning system, then recorded a final decision, giving 2496 paired reads against a radiologist reference standard. Standalone AI sensitivity was 75.6%, falling to 46.2% for subtle fractures, below the radiographers’ baseline sensitivity of 91.6%. Radiographers’ baseline accuracy was high (97.6%; specificity 99.0%) and improved modestly with AI assistance (98.0%; exact McNemar p = 0.0064). With AI assistance, radiographers corrected 11 errors and introduced 1, a net gain of 10 cases. Subgroup gains were directionally consistent but not significant after correction. Radiographers changed their decision in only 11 of 729 discordant cases, and most negative interactions were correct AI recommendations not adopted. No or incomplete AI output was returned for 8.8% of acquired examinations. AI assistance delivered a small, selective benefit arising from complementary rather than superior algorithmic performance. Operational reliability proved as consequential as diagnostic accuracy, and behavioural inferences rest on few events. Downstream clinical outcomes were not measured.

title: Scalable drift monitoring in medical imaging AI
abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into clinical medical imaging has advanced diagnostics but also poses challenges in maintaining long-term reliability as input data change. To address this, we present MMC+, a modular framework for scalable drift monitoring that builds on our CheXstray framework for real-time drift detection using multi-modal data concordance (MMC). MMC+ provides a flexible architecture that enables cost-effective continuous performance monitoring in real-world healthcare settings. The framework’s capabilities include aggregating information from multiple data streams using statistical tests or distance metrics, leveraging foundation model embeddings to remove the need for site-specific encoder training, and quantifying uncertainty to better communicate drift significance. Validated with data from Massachusetts General Hospital during the COVID-19 pandemic, MMC+ effectively detects significant data shifts that correlate with performance changes and indicates when AI systems may deviate from acceptable performance bounds. The code for MMC+ is publicly available (Link: https://github.com/FJDorfner/MedImaging-ModelDriftMonitoring/tree/MMC_plus ), promoting broader adoption of AI solutions in clinical settings. Our framework significantly advances drift detection while promoting transparency and collaboration in clinical AI research.

title: An interpretable graph reasoning framework for enhanced diagnosis in fundus fluorescein angiography
abstract: Fundus fluorescein angiography (FFA) is the gold standard for diagnosing retinal vascular diseases. However, interpretable artificial intelligence (AI) systems for FFA image analysis that align with clinicians’ reasoning processes and real-world diagnostic workflows remain scarce. In this study, we introduce an interpretable graph reasoning framework, FFA-RGNet, that explicitly models the temporal patterns of fine-grained lesions across imaging phases and anatomical locations for disease diagnosis from sequential FFA images. FFA-RGNet was trained and validated on a large, fine-grained, multi-center dataset consisting of 25,312 FFA images from 2651 patients. FFA-RGNet outperformed nine baseline models on the internal test set, achieving an F1-score of 95.38% (95% CI: 92.24%–97.88%), and demonstrated consistent performance across multi-center and prospective validation datasets. Its diagnostic performance not only surpassed that of ophthalmologists, residents and ophthalmology students, but also improved their diagnostic F1-score by 7.48% to 14.11% when used as an assistive tool. Comprehensive inference analysis further revealed its superior ability to correctly recognize fine-grained semantic entities, and to learn stable, disease-specific graph reasoning patterns aligned with clinical knowledge. These results suggest that FFA-RGNet enables accurate diagnosis with interpretable reasoning progresses, highlighting its strong potential as a reliable AI system for FFA interpretation and clinical decision support.

title: Mobile application-based digital therapeutics for frozen shoulder rehabilitation: a single-center, randomized controlled pilot study
abstract: Digital therapeutics offer promising solutions for frozen shoulder rehabilitation. This single-center, assessor-blinded, randomized controlled pilot trial compared an AI-based digital therapeutic application (ANAPA ME) with YouTube-based home exercises in 18 patients with frozen shoulder. Following baseline assessments, patients were allocated to the digital therapeutics (DTx) or conventional rehabilitation (CON) group, received a single ultrasound-guided intra-articular corticosteroid injection, and completed a 12-week exercise program. Assessments at weeks 0, 2, 4, 8, and 12 included passive range of motion (ROM), Visual Analog Scale (VAS), Constant Shoulder Score (CSS), Shoulder Pain and Disability Index (SPADI), and EuroQol-5 Dimension-5 Level (EQ-5D-5L). At 12 weeks, the DTx group achieved significantly greater side external rotation ROM ( p = 0.04) and improvement from baseline ( p = 0.042). EQ-5D-5L showed a significant group × time interaction ( p = 0.048), with greater improvement from baseline in the DTx group ( p = 0.013). No significant between-group differences were observed in VAS, SPADI, or CSS. These findings suggest that AI-based digital therapeutics may offer preliminary advantages in side external rotation ROM and health-related quality of life over conventional video-based exercises, though confirmation in larger trials is needed. This trial was registered with the Clinical Research Information Service, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency (registration number: PRE20250113-001) on January 13, 2025.

title: Performance of artificial intelligence for fracture detection: an umbrella review and second-order-meta-analysis
abstract: Fractures affect approximately 178 million people annually, and artificial intelligence (AI) tools for fracture detection are increasingly approved by regulators. We conducted an umbrella review and second-order meta-analysis (PROSPERO CRD42024516414), searching six databases to 4/06/2025 for systematic reviews or meta-analyses of AI fracture detection using any imaging modality. Screening, extraction, and quality assessment were performed in duplicate. We assessed review quality using AMSTAR-2, primary-study overlap using corrected covered area, and certainty using GRADE. Fifty reviews were included (25 systematic reviews and 25 meta-analyses; 387 primary studies). Twenty-one meta-analyses (269 primary studies) contributed to second-order meta-analysis, with slight overall overlap (4.31%). Pooled AI sensitivity was 0.897 (95% CI 0.882–0.911; 95% prediction interval 0.753–0.962) and specificity 0.904 (95% CI 0.891–0.916; prediction interval 0.824 to 0.950). Comparative evidence showed no consistent differences for AI, clinicians, and AI-assisted clinicians: however, this data was sparse and inconclusive. No review reported adverse events or other safety outcomes. Certainty was very low/low for almost all outcomes; all meta-analyses were rated critically low/low on AMSTAR-2. Although published estimates suggest high diagnostic accuracy, real-world and comparative performance remain uncertain. Prospective external validation, multi-reader-multi-case studies, and randomised trials are needed before broad clinical adoption.

title: A physics-informed peripheral hemodynamic digital twin for personalized estimation of arterial stiffness
abstract: Arterial stiffness, commonly assessed by pulse wave velocity (PWV), is an important biomarker of cardiovascular risk, yet conventional PWV measurements require dual-site recordings that limit scalability in clinical settings. Here we introduce a physics-informed peripheral hemodynamic digital twin framework for estimating central-brachial arterial stiffness from a single brachial pressure waveform. Using our laboratory-developed cuff device, high-resolution brachial pulse waveforms were collected in a cohort of 118 subjects. The digital twin then personalizes a reduced-order wave propagation model through PDE-constrained optimization, generating a compact parameter space that encodes ventricular–vascular characteristics relevant to stiffness. Incorporating digital-twin-derived parameters improved PWV estimation on a blind test cohort ( r = 0.67, RMSE = 1.12 m/s) compared with a baseline model using only age and blood pressure ( r = 0.22, RMSE = 1.90 m/s). These results indicate that physics-informed digital twins can enable scalable, noninvasive assessment of vascular aging from accessible peripheral waveforms.

title: Implementation strategies for digital relapse prevention in schizophrenia identified during a randomized controlled trial
abstract: Digital mental health technologies hold promise, yet their integration into routine care remains challenging. This study reports findings from an implementation workshop conducted midway through an ongoing multi-site randomized controlled trial (RCT) evaluating a smartphone-based relapse prevention app for patients with schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder. Sixteen stakeholders, including developers, researchers, and clinicians, discussed experiences and barriers using a semi-structured agenda, incorporating prior feedback from three focus groups with people with lived experience, and analyzed the discussions using an adopted R(E)-AIM framework (Reach, Adoption, Implementation, and Maintenance). Findings highlight the need for structural, technical, and personnel adjustments to support sustainable implementation. Key recommendations include integrating digital tools into discharge planning, enhancing interdisciplinary collaboration, delegating digital responsibilities, and streamlining technical workflows to facilitate seamless adoption. These insights inform feasibility considerations and strategic requirements for digital interventions in severe mental illness, offering guidance for future RCTs and practice-oriented integration of digital therapeutics in psychiatric care.

title: Platform evaluation and lessons learned with IT-supported patient recruitment
abstract: Recruiting participants for clinical trials is a challenge, often limited by inefficient methods for identifying eligible candidates. Clinical trial recruitment support systems (CTRSS) can enhance recruitment efficiency by leveraging data from electronic health records (EHR). We evaluated two CTRSS—recruIT and KAS+—to quantify their real-world impact on enrollment. Within the German MIRACUM consortium, we conducted a multicenter segmented interrupted time-series (ITS) evaluation across six university hospitals. Twenty-nine trials contributed 814 observation weeks spanning a control phase (usual practice) and an intervention phase (CTRSS active). Weekly enrollments were compared using segmented negative binomial mixed models estimating level and slope changes at implementation, complemented by Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. A criteria revision covariate captured iterative refinement of computable cohort definitions. In pooled ITS analyses, we observed neither a statistically significant immediate level change nor a statistically significant post-implementation slope change in weekly enrollments. Effects were highly heterogeneous across trials and specialties; implemented eligibility logic most often relied on diagnosis, age, and visit data, while laboratory values and structured observations were seldom available. Higher values of the criteria revision covariate were associated with higher recruitment in some settings, with the most exploratory signal observed at the single KAS+ site. Despite the potential benefits of CTRSS, their effectiveness depends on careful customization and implementation. Overall, our findings suggest that CTRSS impact is context-dependent and that measurable benefit is more likely driven by iterative computable phenotyping and local workflow fit rather than a simple “switch-on” effect. Context-specific adaptation and continual revision of eligibility logic appear critical to realizing benefit. Future studies should reduce trial heterogeneity, strengthen compliance incentives, and employ granular outcomes, such as identification-to-enrollment latency, to better capture workflow-mediated effects.

title: Interpretable graph learning of spatial TME patterns in digital pathology for gastric cancer prognosis
abstract: Current gastric cancer (GC) risk stratification, based on TNM staging and molecular subtypes, often fails to capture intratumoral heterogeneity driving variable outcomes. Although the tumor microenvironment (TME) spatial architecture within histopathological images holds critical prognostic value, quantifying these interactions remains challenging. We present the Graph-based Tumor Microenvironment Aggregation (GTMA) framework, an interpretable deep learning approach modeling whole-slide images as spatial graphs to decipher tissue interactions. Validated in a large cohort ( n = 1871) and TCGA-STAD dataset ( n = 213), the GTMA-derived Risk Score (RS) provided prognostic information complementary to TNM staging and clinical models. Notably, the RS stratified patients into distinct risk groups within identical TNM stages and molecular subtypes, identifying high-risk patients traditionally overlooked. Integrative analysis revealed high-RS tumors feature a fibroblast-dominant, immune-excluded phenotype and distinct stromal spatial patterns. By linking digital pathology to biological TME patterns, GTMA offers a robust, interpretable AI tool for individualized prognostic risk stratification and precision oncology in GC.

title: AnySleep: a channel-agnostic deep learning system for high-resolution sleep staging in multi-center cohorts
abstract: Sleep is essential for health, yet studying its dynamics requires manual sleep staging, a labor-intensive step in research and clinical care. Across centers, polysomnography (PSG) recordings are traditionally scored in 30-s epochs for pragmatic, not physiological, reasons and vary in electrode count, montage, and subject characteristics. These constraints challenge harmonized multi-center studies and the discovery of robust biomarkers on shorter timescales. We present AnySleep, a deep neural network that scores sleep from any electroencephalography (EEG) or electrooculography (EOG) data at adjustable temporal resolutions. We trained and validated the model on over 20,000 overnight recordings (>200,000 h of EEG and EOG) from 28 datasets across multiple clinics to promote robust generalization across sites. The model attains state-of-the-art performance and surpasses or equals established baselines at 30-s epochs. Performance improves with more channels, yet remains strong when EOG is absent, or only EOG or single EEG derivations (frontal, central, or occipital) are available. On sub-30-s timescales, the model captures short wake intrusions consistent with arousals and improves the prediction of pathophysiological conditions (obstructive sleep apnea, narcolepsy type 1, insomnia) over 30-s scoring. We make the model publicly available to facilitate large-scale studies with heterogeneous electrode setups and accelerate biomarker discovery in sleep.

title: Accuracy and impact of an AI safety system for missed specialist referrals in primary care
abstract: Missed specialist referrals in primary care pose substantial health and medico-legal risks, yet remain poorly understood. We developed an AI-supported safety system (MR-AI) to identify missed referrals from consultation notes, evaluated in a quasi-experimental study across seven primary care clinics in Singapore. MR-AI scanned ~25,000 notes weekly for referral intent without a corresponding order, achieving an estimated sevenfold increase in weekly missed referral detection (4.7 percentage point level increase; 95% CI 0.024–0.069; p < 0.001). Of 428 cases flagged, 225 were clinician-verified, alongside 31 patient-reported cases, yielding 256 total detections. MR-AI demonstrated 99.9% specificity and 48.8% sensitivity. In a blinded one-week comparison against seven physician reviewers, MR-AI achieved a PPV of 61.8% versus a human confirmation rate of 51.8% across 83 flagged cases, while requiring approximately 41 fewer projected staff-hours. AI-enabled surveillance substantially assisted in missed referral detection, though sustainable improvement will require complementary preventive workflow changes and future cost-effectiveness assessment.

title: Interpretability-driven feature engineering enables compact and accurate multi-outcome risk stratification at hospitalization for chronic hepatitis B
abstract: Clinical artificial intelligence (AI) often trades predictive performance against interpretability. This study develops an interpretability-driven feature engineering framework for multi-outcome risk stratification at hospitalization for chronic hepatitis B. A total of 36,024 hospitalization records from 22,001 patients were included. The framework integrating SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based main and interaction effects was used to construct compact machine learning models for classifying disease non-progression, liver cirrhosis (LC), and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). SHAP main effects selected the top 15 features per outcome; TreeSHAP interactions selected four pairwise terms. Performance was evaluated using patient-level data splitting, temporal validation, and independent external validation, with calibration and decision-curve analyses. The full-feature models achieved superior discrimination (AUCs: 0.927, 0.897, and 0.899) for classifying hospitalization-recorded disease non-progression, LC, and HCC, respectively. The corresponding compact models maintained strong discrimination (AUCs: 0.911, 0.882, and 0.890) with 80.8% fewer features. Interaction models yielded subtle AUC shifts (AUCs: 0.912, 0.881, and 0.891) while characterizing potential clinical joint-effect patterns. Temporal validation yielded AUCs of 0.863, 0.827, and 0.847, while external validation yielded AUCs of 0.829, 0.865, and 0.827, respectively. The framework produced compact and transparent models for contemporaneous risk stratification in clinical practice, seamlessly uniting predictive accuracy with multi-level interpretability.

title: Understanding clinical reasoning variability in medical large language models: a mechanistic interpretability study
abstract: Medical large language models achieving high benchmark accuracy exhibit unexplained variability in clinical tasks, producing errors that clinicians cannot safeguard against. We evaluated clinical reasoning stability in GPT-5, MedGemma-27B-Text-IT, and OpenBioLLM-Llama3-70B using 3035 systematic perturbations from physician-validated oncology SOAP, brief vignette, and MIMIC cases. We trained sparse autoencoders on 1 billion tokens from 50,000 MIMIC-IV clinical notes to decompose their internal representation. We find models exhibit dramatic reasoning instability, shifting staging accuracy by over 50% based solely on prompt format, or generating definitive staging in clinically insufficient scenarios. Sparse autoencoder analysis revealed hierarchical encoding in MedGemma, where high-magnitude features encode lexical identity and low-magnitude features encode contextual meaning. OpenBioLLM distributes information uniformly. We demonstrate that these internal encoding structures differentially affect retrieval and reasoning interventions, suggesting interventions effective for one architecture may harm another. These results motivate architecture-specific safety validation as a component of pre-deployment evaluation for medical LLMs.

title: Predicting persistent fever in patients with cancer receiving antibiotics: a machine learning approach
abstract: Persistent fever after initiating intravenous antibiotics is common in hospitalized patients with cancer and often leads to additional imaging and antimicrobial escalation. Early identification of patients unlikely to remain febrile could provide additional information during clinical reassessment. We developed and externally validated machine learning models to predict persistent fever 48–72 h after antibiotic initiation using electronic health records from two academic hospitals. Adult cancer patients with fever within 24–48 h of treatment were included. Models incorporated demographics, comorbidities, laboratory results, vital signs, and temperature patterns. The best-performing model achieved an AUROC of 0.82 (95% CI 0.79–0.84) internally and 0.78 (95% CI 0.77–0.79) externally. Temperature-related variables were the dominant predictors. Decision curve analysis demonstrated positive net benefit across much of the evaluated threshold range. Retrospective assessment suggested that approximately one quarter of antibiotic escalations and chest CT scans occurred in patients correctly predicted not to remain febrile, highlighting the potential contextual value of fever predictions. These findings indicate that short-term fever persistence can be predicted with clinically meaningful accuracy using routine data. However, clinical use should be limited to an adjunctive role rather than standalone rule-out decision-making, and prospective studies are required to evaluate safety, clinician uptake, and real-world impact.

title: Generation of synthetic clinical text: a systematic review
abstract: Generating medical synthetic text represents an effective solution for clinical NLP issues like sparsity and privacy. This paper conducts a systematic review on synthetic clinical text generation by formulating quantitative analysis to three research questions concerning the generation’s purpose, generation techniques, and the evaluation methods. We searched four databases including PubMed, Scopus, ScienceDirect and Web of Science for publications associated with the topic and identified 87 relevant articles out of 1148. Results showed that the generation purposes were dedicated to Trustworthy, Medical Assistance, and Language Resource themes. Prompting LLMs was the main source of synthetic text (40 articles). GPTs were the main predominant technique used to generate the text (63 articles), especially ChatGPT (47 articles). Additionally, there were four main aspects of evaluation, including similarity, privacy, structure, and utility, where utility was the prevailing method for assessment (52 articles). The synthetic medical text empowered data augmentation and clinical documentation. Using text alteration, controlling real text portions, and federated learning, generative models can produce privacy-preserving medical text. This accelerates the development of new digital health applications.

title: Predicting different dimensions of fatigue from speech data: a longitudinal study in shift workers
abstract: Shift work, or working outside of normal circadian cycles, is associated with both experience of fatigue and poorer long-term physical and mental health. However, current methods for assessing fatigue present several barriers to building understanding of how these risks develop over time within individuals. Here, we explore the potential of momentary speech activity-based fatigue measurement in a large, multi-lingual cohort of shift workers, using an intensive longitudinal study design (twice-daily measurement over two weeks in N = 1197 individuals from six different countries). Paralinguistic speech features were used to predict different aspects of acute and chronic fatigue at each study time-point, with performance assessed in unseen (held-out) data. In the cross-sectional analysis, good (close to or exceeding current state-of-the-art) performance was achieved for both current sleep deprivation and self-reported sleepiness levels. The within-user analysis revealed robust increases in performance, yielding the ability to detect more subjective aspects of fatigue such as pervasive physical and mental exhaustion. These findings offer preliminary support for the utility of using brief momentary speech samples as a low-burden, acceptable, and reliable measure of different aspects of fatigue in high-risk populations such as shift workers.

title: Cost-effectiveness analysis of digital medicine support models for alcohol use disorder
abstract: Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a major public health issue yet often under-addressed in primary care. Digital health interventions offer scalable support, but health systems require economic data to guide implementation decision-making. In a randomized clinical trial involving 558 participants registered at clinicaltrials.gov (NCT04011644; July 3, 2019), we compared three support models built on a shared digital medicine platform: self-monitored use (SM), peer-supported use (PS), and clinically integrated use (CI). We estimated delivery costs and effectiveness based on reductions in heavy drinking days. Annualized reductions in heavy drinking days were 42.4, 40.2, and 48.3 days per patient for SM, PS, and CI models, with per-patient costs of $162, $524, and $802, respectively. Average cost-effectiveness was $3.8 (SM), $13.0 (PS), and $16.6 (CI); PS was dominated, and the ICER for CI versus SM was $107.9. When downstream healthcare utilization was included, results suggested that more intensive support may be economically advantageous. Modeling implementation at scale showed that PS becomes cost-efficient for large patient populations. These findings highlight that no single model is universally optimal: health systems may benefit from offering multiple support levels to match patient preferences and organizational capacity.

title: The TEMPO program and the future of digital mental health regulation in the US
abstract: The high burden of traditional FDA clearance drives many novel, AI-enabled mental health devices into unregulated consumer markets. The new FDA-CMS TEMPO pilot program establishes a vital regulatory middle ground, allowing companies to commercialize using a Quality Management System without immediate premarket authorization. This commentary explores how TEMPO serves as a sandbox for real-world data, offering a blueprint to reshape the future of US digital health regulation.

title: RETBind: a patient-level multimodal foundation model for unified cross-modal retinal representation learning
abstract: Medical artificial intelligence (AI) holds considerable promise across a wide range of ophthalmic tasks, offering a practical path to patient-level diagnostic support. Foundation models further extend this potential by learning generalizable representations from large-scale unlabeled data, alleviating the burden of extensive manual annotation. However, existing ophthalmic foundation models largely rely on single-modality or modality-specific encoders, failing to capture patient-level cross-modal correspondence in real-world multimodal clinical workflows. To address these gaps, we propose RETBind, a patient-level multimodal foundation model with a unified encoder that explicitly learns cross-modal correspondence from paired clinical imaging using patient-level paired optical coherence tomography (OCT) and ultra-widefield (UWF) fundus imaging. This patient-level paired pretraining strategy enables the model to learn unified cross-modal representations of complementary information, improv-ing performance and robustness beyond single-modality approaches. Across nine benchmark datasets spanning ocular disease classification and segmentation tasks, RETBind achieved consistent improvements, particularly enhancing AUPR in clinically relevant imbalanced settings. Exploratory analyses further examined the potential of RETBind for systemic disease prediction from retinal imaging, collectively highlighting its ability to learn unified cross-modal representations within a single shared encoder, enabling direct interaction between modalities and supporting transfer across diverse retinal imaging tasks.

title: Emerging applications of machine learning and AI for predictive modeling in precision medicine
abstract: Pure data-driven artificial intelligence (AI) is insufficient for clinical adoption. This editorial summarizes 31 papers showing that precision medicine requires integrating structural domain knowledge before model training. We identify three necessary transitions: anchoring algorithms in biological laws for mechanistic interpretability; designing collaborative, human-centered clinical interfaces; and scaling equitable, population-level interventions. These shifts advance medical AI from technical novelty toward trustworthy, clinically grounded, and ethically deployed foundational science.

title: A multimodal tool-augmented agent for evidence-based clinical decision support in longitudinal AMD follow-up
abstract: Clinical management of age-related macular degeneration (AMD) requires longitudinal decisions on disease activity, treatment response, and anti-VEGF injection intervals. These decisions depend on integrating multimodal retinal imaging findings across visits, yet manual synthesis is time-consuming and may omit relevant information, limiting transparency and consistency in follow-up planning. Large language models (LLMs) have been explored to summarize longitudinal AMD information, but existing approaches may lack explicit quantitative grounding and evidence attribution, reducing their auditability in clinical decision support. To address these limitations, we developed AMDagent, an evidence-grounded clinical agent that integrates quantitative imaging analysis with guideline retrieval to generate structured, clinician-facing decision-support outputs. The system links longitudinal imaging findings to actionable management considerations while preserving traceable evidence sources. In a 20-case proof-of-concept evaluation of curated longitudinal AMD cases, AMDagent was rated clinically appropriate in 92.0% of predefined decision-support units under expert adjudication. In addition, 83.3% of audited major clinical claims were explicitly grounded in tool-derived quantitative measurements and/or retrieved guideline evidence, enabling clinician verification. These preliminary findings suggest that evidence-grounded, clinician-facing agents may support more transparent and auditable longitudinal AMD decision support, although larger prospective multi-center studies are needed to assess generalizability and clinical utility.

title: Cross-paradigm audit of large language model judges for clinical text evaluation
abstract: Large language models are increasingly being used to evaluate clinical texts, a concept known as LLM-as-a-judge. However, most of the existing evidence focuses on English data and uses pooled agreement metrics that obscure clinically relevant failure modes. This study audited six open-weight models against expert judges on four German clinical datasets covering report and nursing documentation summarization, discharge summary generation, and patient letter generation. The models were evaluated across three paradigms and four prompt configurations. Alignment with experts varied by criterion and corpus, and no configuration proved reliable across paradigms. All judges exhibited position and identity bias. Substituting LLM-as-a-judge for the expert panel shifted 57.2% of pointwise categories, swapped 41.7% of pairwise winners, missed 10.2% of clinical errors, and inverted clinical priorities by overrating the criteria succinct and accurate. Therefore, LLM-as-a-judge is not a safe substitute for experts in German clinical text evaluations, and deployment thresholds should follow decision-impact analysis for LLM-as-a-judge in clinical contexts.

title: Digital and hybrid interventions for subacute and chronic low back pain: component network meta-analysis
abstract: Digital and hybrid interventions combining exercise, education, and psychological components are increasingly used for low back pain (LBP), but it remains unclear which components and combinations drive efficacy. We conducted a prospectively registered component network meta-analysis (CNMA) to evaluate their efficacy and safety for non-specific LBP. Six databases and two trial registries were searched to May 2025. Data on disability, pain intensity, and adverse events were analysed using a Bayesian random-effects CNMA. Of 2809 records, 56 reports of 46 studies (6717 participants; 80% chronic low back pain) were included. Hybrid interventions combining digital and in-person exercise with in-person psychological components (MD: –22.21; 95%-CrI: –34.11 to –10.67), digital and in-person exercise (MD: –15.75; 95%-CrI: –22.79 to –8.80), or digital exercise with physiotherapy (MD: –13.17; 95%-CrI: –21.18 to –5.16) reduced disability versus no intervention at short-term (minimal clinically important difference (MCID): 4.92/100 Oswestry Disability Index). Digital and in-person exercise (MD: -1.76; 95%-CrI: -2.62; -0.87) and combined digital exercise training with in-person education (MD: -1.73; 95%-CrI: -2.71; -0.83) improved pain intensity beyond the MCID (0.82/10 numeric pain rating scale). No serious adverse events were noted. Multicomponent hybrid interventions appear safe and may provide clinically meaningful improvements for chronic LBP.
